text: Americas Technology: Semiconductors: EDA: Poised to begin capturing Agentic AI value with potential revenue acceleration—Buy CDNS, SNPS

Consensus has viewed Cadence and Synopsys as “defensive” 12%-15% growers at best, and potential victims of AI disruption at worst—with the stocks having lagged the SOXX by \~120 points in the past year. However, our new analysis suggests the shift toward custom AI silicon has exacerbated a structural shortage of chip design engineers that EDA companies are uniquely positioned to monetize with Agentic AI—an incremental opportunity we estimate at \~\$3.7bn/year by 2030, which is not reflected in Street estimates and may start to be evident as early as 2H26. We believe consensus reflects the “pre-AI” version of the industry as growth is about to inflect, creating an opportunity in the stocks today.

\- AI customer chip demand could drive a global shortage of \~72,000 chip designers by 2030. A key industry benchmark study (SIA/BCG, 2022) projected a \~23k shortfall in US chip designers before generative AI. Since then, hyperscalers and AI labs have launched custom silicon programs requiring at least \~2,500 designers. Meanwhile, the supply of human designers grows at just 2%-3% annually. We estimate AI design tools can add \~48k agentic engineer-equivalents by 2030, which can partially close this gap.

We size the Agentic AI revenue opportunity for EDA at \~\$3.7bn annually by 2030 based on modest adoption assumptions. We estimate “Copilot-style” AI EDA tools could price at \~\$25k per engineer annually, relative to the \~\$90–\$100k customers spend in EDA per seat. We also think autonomous agents, which both EDA vendors will launch in 2026-27, could handle up to 30% of work by 2030 at \~\$50k per agent—or \~25% of the fully-loaded cost of a human design engineer.

■ Street numbers reflect essentially none — and we believe initial proof points could be evident within months. Consensus models both companies decelerating revenue growth from here, implying zero credit for this new Agentic layer. We estimate that this opportunity could lift Cadence’s revenue growth from \~13% to the mid-20% range (+\$2.30 of EPS by 2030) and Synopsys to \~20% (+\$2.20). 2H results could provide the first evidence of this growth opportunity. If agentic AI tool adoption gains traction, we believe CDNS/SNPS could re-rate in terms of faster growth rates and higher multiples.

We reiterate our Buy ratings on CDNS and SNPS. Our CDNS 12-month target moves to \$470 from \$410 (\~22% upside), still based on 45X on normalized EPS earnings of \$10.50 (from \$9.10 on more visibility). We see \~35% upside for SNPS.

Chip design labor shortage could drive a material EDA revenue opportunity through 2030

Bottom Line: The semiconductor industry has a long-standing labor problem, with the world producing new chip designers at just 2%-3% a year—yielding \~255k engineers by 2030—relative to the 325k design engineers we estimate the industry will require to service surging AI-driven demand.

According to a 2022 industry workforce study by the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) and Boston Consulting Group (BCG), as of 2021 the industry already expected a shortfall of roughly 23,000 chip designers by 2030. Since that study (which predates the 2023 generative AI boom), hyperscalers and AI labs have quickly built their own chip programs, while merchant chipmakers have cut design cycles from two years to one. Layering in that incremental demand implies a global shortage of \~70k designers by 2030 based on our estimates. As AI design tools are the only supply response available in the short term, our estimates suggest they could augment the industry by \~48k engineer-equivalents by 2030—enough to cover the shortage the industry had five years ago, but not the demand the AI boom has since created. We believe Cadence and Synopsys—the two market leaders in EDA tools—are best positioned to convert a structural labor deficit into a new revenue stream—roughly \~\$3.7bn of incremental, consumption-priced AI software by 2030 (\~\$11bn in cumulative revenue in 2026-30), on top of a \~\$14bn base of core EDA revenues, none of which is reflected in Street numbers today.

We expect a material AI revenue opportunity for EDA software, even on conservative assumptions

Bottom Line: Our model assumptions are deliberately conservative despite the significant upside potential offered by AI tools in an industry constrained by labor supply. Even so, our estimates equate to \$3.7bn of incremental annualized AI revenue by 2030.

Our analysis begins with the global population of chip designers, where we isolate the roles AI tools can already help augment (such as verification, physical design, RTL) and exclude what they still cannot. We quantify two distinct revenue layers: (1) AI augmentation or copilot-style tools for existing human engineers (adoption starts at 20%-40% of leading-edge designs where AI is already used today, priced at \~\$25k per engineer, or a \~20% pricing uplift on AI-enhanced renewals already observed); (2) Autonomous AI agents that compensate for the engineers who cannot be hired (we assume agents perform just 30% of that unfilled work by 2030, priced at \~\$50k per “virtual engineer,” or less than half of the implied value capture). Our forecast relies on what we believe are relatively modest, real-world assumptions (e.g., partial adoption, value-price pricing) yet comfortably compounds to a \~\$3.7B annual market by 2030.

Still priced for pre-AI growth — despite the AI inflection now in sight

Bottom Line: We believe the market has largely treated EDA companies as bystanders in the AI trade—as defensive, stable growers at best and as victims of AI disruption at worst—with the SOXX delivering a \~140% TTM return while CDNS gained \~20% and SNPS traded sideways. We now see a major catalyst on the horizon as agentic AI products enter the market in the coming quarters.

According to Street estimates (Visible Alpha), Cadence is seemingly modeled on the same growth algorithm it has been—\~8% volume growth plus \~6% pricing, decelerating to \~13% by 2028—with AI apparently driving zero contribution (Exhibit 9). Layering in our AI upside estimates could accelerate revenue growth to the mid-to-high 20% range for CDNS and \~20% for SNPS, driving incremental EPS of \~\$2.30 and \~\$2.20 by 2030, respectively. Critically, this revenue would reflect sustainable, high-quality growth from consumption-priced software amid a structural labor shortage, delivered through the same incumbent tools the industry already uses on a daily basis. In addition, we believe agents would only work in conjunction with the vendors' own simulation and signoff engines. With CDNS trading at \~45X NTM EPS (and SNPS at \~35X) on the assumption that neither grows significantly faster than mid-double digits in the medium term, we expect significant upside to both names if the first evidence of AI adoption and monetization is demonstrated in the coming quarters.

GS Factor Profile

The GS Factor Profile provides investment context for a stock by comparing key attributes to the market (i.e. our universe of rated stocks) and its sector peers. The four key attributes depicted are: Growth, Financial Returns, Multiple (e.g. valuation) and Integrated (a composite of Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple). Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple are calculated by using normalized ranks for specific metrics for each stock. The normalized ranks for the metrics are then averaged and converted into percentiles for the relevant attribute. The precise calculation of each metric may vary depending on the fiscal year, industry and region, but the standard approach is as follows:

Growth is based on a stock's forward-looking sales growth, EBITDA growth and EPS growth (for financial stocks, only EPS and sales growth), with a higher percentile indicating a higher growth company. Financial Returns is based on a stock's forward-looking ROE, ROCE and CROCI (for financial stocks, only ROE), with a higher percentile indicating a company with higher financial returns. Multiple is based on a stock's forward-looking P/E, P/B, price/dividend (P/D), EV/EBITDA, EV/FCF and EV/Debt Adjusted Cash Flow (DACF) (for financial stocks, only P/E, P/B and P/D), with a higher percentile indicating a stock trading at a higher multiple. The Integrated percentile is calculated as the average of the Growth percentile, Financial Returns percentile and (100% - Multiple percentile).

Financial Returns and Multiple use the GS analyst forecasts at the fiscal year-end at least three quarters in the future. Growth uses inputs for the fiscal year at least seven quarters in the future compared with the year at least three quarters in the future (on a per-share basis for all metrics).
For a more detailed description of how we calculate the GS Factor Profile, please contact your GS representative.
M&A Rank

Across our global coverage, we examine stocks using an M&A framework, considering both qualitative factors and quantitative factors (which may vary across sectors and regions) to incorporate the potential that certain companies could be acquired. We then assign a M&A rank as a means of scoring companies under our rated coverage from 1 to 3, with 1 representing high (30%-50%) probability of the company becoming an acquisition target, 2 representing medium (15%-30%) probability and 3 representing low (0%-15%) probability. For companies ranked 1 or 2, in line with our standard departmental guidelines we incorporate an M&A component into our target price. M&A rank of 3 is considered immaterial and therefore does not factor into our price target, and may or may not be discussed in research.
